0.text: A BI-RADS Category 3 assessment indicates a finding with a less than 2% likelihood of malignancy. The recommended management is short-interval follow-up mammography at 6 months, followed by bilateral mammography at 12 months and 24 months. If stability is demonstrated at 24 months, the assessment can be downgraded to Category 2 (benign).

1.text: Category 3 findings should not be biopsied as the initial management. Biopsy may be appropriate if the patient has anxiety, if follow-up is not feasible, or if the lesion changes during follow-up.

2.text: Common Category 3 findings include: a group of round punctate calcifications, a non-palpable round or oval circumscribed mass on a first mammogram, and focal asymmetry without associated suspicious features.

3.text: A BI-RADS Category 4 assessment indicates a finding for which biopsy should be considered. Category 4 encompasses a wide range of malignancy probability (2%–95%) and is subdivided:

4.section: BI-RADS Category 5: Highly Suggestive of Malignancy
4.text: A BI-RADS Category 5 assessment indicates a finding that is highly suggestive of malignancy, with a greater than 95% probability of malignancy. Biopsy is required. A benign pathology result should be considered discordant; excision or re-biopsy is required.

5.section: BI-RADS Category 5: Highly Suggestive of Malignancy
5.text: Category 5 findings include: spiculated high-density masses, pleomorphic calcifications in a linear or branching distribution, and a combination of highly suspicious features.

6.text: Radiological–pathological concordance is the process of comparing the imaging findings with the biopsy pathology result. A benign pathology result is concordant if it specifically explains the imaging abnormality (e.g., a fibroadenoma explaining a well-defined oval mass). A benign pathology result is discordant if it does not explain the imaging finding. Discordant results require multidisciplinary review and typically lead to re-biopsy or surgical excision.

7.section: What Happens After an Abnormal Mammogram?
7.text:
1. Additional diagnostic mammography views or breast ultrasound may be recommended to further characterise the finding.
2. If a biopsy is recommended (Category 4 or 5), image-guided core needle biopsy is the standard procedure.
3. Biopsy results are reviewed in a multidisciplinary meeting including radiology, pathology, and surgery.
4. If malignancy is confirmed, staging and treatment planning are initiated.
5. If biopsy shows benign concordant pathology, follow-up imaging is scheduled per the BI-RADS protocol.

8.section: What Happens After an Abnormal Mammogram?
8.text: An AI risk estimate does not replace this clinical workflow. A risk estimate of any level does not bypass the need for clinical assessment, imaging interpretation by a radiologist, and — where indicated — biopsy.

9.text: Margin refers to the border of a mass as visualised on mammography. Margin characterisation is the single most predictive feature for distinguishing benign from malignant masses in the mammographic mammographic Masses dataset (Elter, 2007).

10.text: Density describes the X-ray attenuation of the mass relative to an equivalent volume of fibroglandular tissue.

11.text: A mammographic mass is a space-occupying lesion seen in two different projections on a mammogram. A mass has a three-dimensional shape that differentiates it from a density, which is visible in only one projection. Masses are characterised by their shape, margin, and density.

12.text: A mammogram is an X-ray of the breast. It is the primary screening tool for breast cancer detection. Digital mammography uses electronic detectors to convert X-rays into digital images, which can be enhanced and stored electronically. Digital breast tomosynthesis (3D mammography) acquires multiple images at different angles to produce reconstructed cross-sectional images, improving detection in dense breast tissue.

13.text: BI-RADS stands for Breast Imaging Reporting and Data System. It is a standardised reporting system developed by the American College of Radiology (ACR) to reduce variability in mammographic interpretation. BI-RADS provides a structured lexicon for describing findings and a numeric assessment category to guide clinical management.

14.text:
BI-RADS assessment categories range from 0 to 6:
- Category 0: Incomplete — additional imaging needed
- Category 1: Negative — routine screening
- Category 2: Benign — routine screening
- Category 3: Probably benign — short-interval follow-up (6 months)
- Category 4: Suspicious — biopsy should be considered (sub-divided 4A, 4B, 4C)
- Category 5: Highly suggestive of malignancy — biopsy required
- Category 6: Known biopsy-proven malignancy

15.text: A fibroadenoma is the most common benign breast tumour, typically presenting as a well-defined, oval or round, circumscribed mass in young women. Fibroadenomas may exhibit calcifications on imaging. They do not require treatment unless symptomatic or large.

16.text: A breast cyst is a fluid-filled sac within the breast tissue. Simple cysts are completely anechoic on ultrasound and require no further workup. Complicated and complex cysts may require further imaging or aspiration.

17.text: Fine needle aspiration is a minimally invasive diagnostic procedure in which a thin needle is inserted into a mass to extract cells for cytological analysis. The Wisconsin Breast Cancer Diagnostic (WDBC) dataset features were computed from FNA specimens.

18.text: A breast biopsy is the removal of a tissue sample from a breast abnormality for pathological examination. Image-guided core needle biopsy (CNB) is the standard of care for evaluating suspicious mammographic masses. A biopsy is required to confirm or exclude malignancy. An AI risk estimate is not a substitute for biopsy.

19.text: Nuclear features describe the characteristics of cell nuclei observed under microscopy, including radius, texture, perimeter, area, smoothness, compactness, concavity, concave points, symmetry, and fractal dimension. The WDBC dataset contains 30 nuclear features computed from FNA images.

20.text: Malignancy probability is the estimated likelihood that a mass represents a cancer, expressed as a percentage. It is derived from the features of the mass and the prior probability of malignancy in the population. A malignancy probability is a statistical estimate, not a diagnosis. Only histopathological examination of biopsy tissue can confirm or exclude malignancy.

21.text: Sensitivity (recall) is the proportion of true positive cases correctly identified. Specificity is the proportion of true negative cases correctly identified. In breast cancer screening, high sensitivity is prioritised to minimise false negatives (missed cancers), sometimes at the cost of lower specificity (more false positives requiring additional workup).

22.text: BreastCare AI is a research and educational prototype that estimates malignancy probability from four structured mammographic features: patient age, mass shape, mass margin, and mass density. It uses a LightGBM model trained on the UCI Mammographic Masses dataset (Elter, 2007) and produces SHAP-based feature attribution to explain its estimates.

23.text: This tool is not a medical device. It has not been cleared or approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) or any other regulatory authority. It is not intended for clinical diagnosis, treatment planning, or as a substitute for radiological interpretation.

24.text: This tool does not process mammogram images. It uses structured numeric features only. Its accuracy is limited by the small size of its training data (860 cases) and the sparsity of its feature set (4 features). Production clinical AI systems use 20 or more descriptors, calcification patterns, and full mammographic image analysis.

25.text: The model was trained on data from a single institution and may not generalise to other screening programmes, imaging equipment, or patient populations. It has not been validated in a prospective clinical trial. Its performance in real-world screening settings is unknown.

26.text: The model returns a point estimate without calibrated confidence intervals. The fixed decision threshold of 0.50 is not optimised for any clinical cost-benefit ratio.

27.text: When the estimated malignancy probability is 65% or higher, this tool displays an enhanced notice. A high probability estimate does not mean a diagnosis of cancer. It means the features you entered are statistically associated with a higher likelihood of malignancy in the training data. Only biopsy and pathological examination can confirm or exclude malignancy.

28.text: If you have received an abnormal mammography result, or if you have concerns about a breast finding, you should consult a qualified radiologist or physician. Do not use this tool's output to make or delay clinical decisions.

29.text: All estimates produced by this tool must be reviewed by a qualified clinician before any clinical action is taken.

30.text: This tool does not collect, store, or transmit personal health information. The feature values entered are used solely to compute and display a risk estimate within your session. No data is retained after the session ends.

31.text: BreastCare AI was developed as an academic research prototype demonstrating the integration of gradient boosted tree models, SHAP explainability, FAISS retrieval-augmented generation, and Google Gemini for educational purposes in the context of breast cancer screening research.
